title: Infra: GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & IaC CI/CD playbook
author: Jordan Lee
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's current infrastructure engineering standards and runbooks for the GPU fleet and capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD build pipelines. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate or change the GPU-backed inference infrastructure.

Goals
- Provide a single, actionable reference for capacity planning and scaling decisions.
- Standardize Terraform module layout, CI/CD gating, and release procedures.
- Define ownership, SLOs, and incident runbooks for GPU infra.

Scope
- GPU fleet provisioning and lifecycle (AWS/GCP/Private clusters).
- Cloud accounts, VPCs, routing, and peering used by inference clusters.
- Terraform modules, versioning, and module registry usage.
- CI/CD pipelines that build, test, and deploy infra modules and cluster changes.
- Runbooks for common operational tasks and incident response.

Ownership and Contacts
- Service owner: infra-platform@redwood.internal (primary oncall rota)
- Owners by area:
  - GPU fleet capacity & autoscaling: @Miguel Rivera
  - Terraform modules & IaC: @Priya Desai
  - CI/CD & build pipelines: @Ava Thompson
  - Cloud accounts & networking: @Liam O'Connell

Key Components (high level)
1) GPU fleet and capacity
- Fleet types: shared-hosted, dedicated-reserved, private-onprem.
- Node types: p4d (A100-40GB equivalent), a10g, and nvlink-enabled variants for KV cache heavy workloads.
- Capacity units: we track provisioned GPUs, available GPU-hours, and headroom (target headroom = 15% baseline, adjustable by region).

2) Cloud accounts & networking
- Account per-environment (prod-us-west-2, prod-eu-west-1, staging, sandbox).
- VPC design: one VPC per region per account, with segmented subnets: management (bastion/API), compute (GPU nodes), data (storage), services (control plane).
- Networking controls: centralized CNI (Calico) with egress NAT gateways and strict security groups limiting SSH/API access.

3) Terraform / IaC modules
- Module registry: internal Terraform registry (module namespace: redwood/infra/*).
- Module layout convention:
  - modules/networking (vpc, subnets, route-tables)
  - modules/gpu-cluster (asg/instance-groups, node-bootstrap, taints/labels)
  - modules/iam (roles, instance-profiles, policies)
  - modules/observability (prometheus, logging, alerting configs)
- Semantic versioning: modules must follow semver; breaking changes require ADR + major version bump.

4) CI/CD and build
- Pipelines: repo-per-module with a shared pipeline template in infra-ci/pipelines/ (DRY and reusable).
- Build stages:
  1. fmt/validate (terraform fmt, tflint, tfsec)
  2. unit/integration (kitchen-terraform or terratest where applicable)
  3. plan (terraform plan with varfiles for envs)
  4. manual-approval (for prod plans)
  5. apply (automated for non-prod; gated for prod via commit to release branch)
- Gate rules: every plan that modifies prod account resources must have 2 approvers and a successful integration test run.

Standards & Conventions
- Branching: trunk-based; feature branches used for changes and merged via PR after CI passes.
- Secrets: stored only in KMS-backed secret manager (no tfvars with secrets in repo).
- State: remote state in encrypted backend (S3 + DynamoDB lock for AWS; GCS + state-locking for GCP). Each environment has its own state bucket and lock table.
- Tagging: all resources must include tags: {"owner":"team", "project":"redwood-inference", "env":"prod|staging|sandbox"}.

Capacity Planning and Sizing
- Metrics to track:
  - GPU utilization (p99/p95/p50) by instance type
  - Queue length and average latency (token throughput) per model route
  - Provisioned vs used GPU-hours (daily)
- Thresholds and alerting:
  - Warning: average cluster GPU utilization > 70% for 30m -> paging to oncall-sre
  - Critical: average cluster GPU utilization > 90% for 15m OR queue latency > 2x target SLO -> critical incident runbook
- Autoscaling policy guidance:
  - Keep conservative cooldown windows for models with bursty inference (default scale-in delay = 10m, scale-out cooldown = 3m).
  - Minimum pool size: ensure at least 3 GPUs per AZ for high-availability; for small clusters, min 2 GPUs with cross-AZ fallback.

Terraform module example (recommended fields)
| Module | Purpose | Required inputs | Outputs | Notes |
|--------|---------|-----------------|---------|-------|
| modules/gpu-cluster | Provision node groups and autoscaling | instance_type, desired_count, min_count, max_count, ami_id, ssh_key | node_group_arn, instance_profile | Use user-data bootstrap to mount kv-cache and join cluster |

CI/CD pipeline template (excerpt)
- .gitlab-ci.yml (shared template usage):
  - validate:
      script:
        - terraform fmt -check
        - tflint --config .tflint.hcl
        - tfsec .
  - plan:
      script:
        - terraform init -backend-config="bucket=${STATE_BUCKET}"
        - terraform plan -var-file="${ENV}.tfvars" -out=plan.tfplan
      artifacts:
        paths:
          - plan.tfplan
  - apply:
      stage: apply
      when: manual
      script:
        - terraform apply "plan.tfplan"

Runbooks (operations excerpts)
1) Scale up GPU capacity (planned maintenance)
1. Open the capacity request ticket in JIRA (project: INFRA) with desired region, instance type, and target date.
2. Run capacity simulation script: infra-tools/plan_capacity.py --region us-west-2 --target-gpus 40 -> produces tfvars delta.
3. Create PR in modules/gpu-cluster repo with updated desired_count or new node pool module invocation.
4. CI will run plan; reviewers: @Miguel Rivera, @Priya Desai. After approvals, merge to release branch and schedule apply during maintenance window.
5. Post-apply checks (see checklist).

Checklist after scale apply:
- Confirm nodes registered with cluster: kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu
- Confirm GPU drivers, nvidia-plugins, and kv-cache mounted: kubectl describe daemonset nvidia-driver | grep Ready
- Monitor GPU utilization and queue latency for 30m.

2) Emergency scaling (unplanned demand spike)
1. Page oncall-sre and oncall-infra with summary (region, model route, observed metrics).
2. Triage: determine whether to increase max_count in the autoscaler or launch an emergency node pool using pre-approved instance types.
3. If immediate capacity required, a senior infra engineer may use the emergency apply job in infra-ci to create a temporary node pool (must be followed by postmortem and cleanup ticket).

Rollback and Upgrade Process for Node Pools
- Preferred: create replacement node pool with new AMI/config, cordon and drain old nodes, and then decommission.
- Avoid in-place upgrades of node AMI for pools with live KV cache unless KV state is replicated.

Testing and Validation
- Unit tests: terratest + go test for infrastructure logic.
- Integration: ephemeral test environment deployment using ephemeral accounts/gen-terraform-state for PR validation.
- Chaos testing: quarterly simulated AZ failure and node preemption drills.

Observability and Dashboards
- Standard dashboards (Grafana): GPU utilization by cluster, queue latency per model route, infra error rates, instance provisioning time.
- Alerts in PagerDuty: infra-alerts-escalation (critical), infra-alerts-warning (non-critical).

Security and Compliance notes
- All IAM changes must be reviewed by the security team.
- KMS keys: use customer-managed keys for Private deployments; hosted uses company-managed keys with restricted access.
- Audit logs: Terraform applies to prod must include plan artifacts for audit retention (retained 90 days).

Change Approval and Release windows
- Prod change window: Mon–Fri 00:00–05:00 UTC (preferred) unless emergency.
- Major changes (networking, routing, large capacity moves) require at least 48h notice and a rollout plan.

Appendices
A) Useful CLI snippets
- Terraform plan for prod:
  export STATE_BUCKET=redwood-prod-infra-state
  terraform init -backend-config="bucket=${STATE_BUCKET}"
  terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan

- Drain GPU node:
  kubectl cordon NODE_NAME
  kubectl drain NODE_NAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force

B) Example tfvars snippet
region = "us-west-2"
cluster_name = "gpu-cluster-prod-usw2"
node_pools = [{"name":"p4d-pool","instance_type":"p4d.24xlarge","min":3,"max":60,"desired":12}]

C) Related documentation
- /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026.json
- /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026.json

D) Revision history
- 2026-02-10: Created by Jordan Lee.
- 2026-02-22: Added CI/CD gating and autoscaling recommendations (review: Priya Desai).
- 2026-03-01: Published, minor clarifications to runbooks (review: Ava Thompson).

If you have questions or need a live walk-through of these procedures, ping the infra Slack channel (#infra-gpu-capacity) or open a PR in infra-ci/.
